title: Samsung to use TSMC technology for Nvidia's next-generation memory chips, Seoul newspaper reports
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Samsung Electronics will use TSMC’s manufacturing technology for a key component of Nvidia’s next generation of custom memory chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday, citing industry sources.

The South Korean company plans to adopt TSMC’s three-nanometre process for the base die in Nvidia’s custom high-bandwidth memory, known as NVHBM. The arrangement would mark Samsung’s first collaboration with the Taiwanese contract chipmaker at the HBM manufacturing stage, according to the newspaper.

Nvidia has asked its three memory suppliers, Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology, to use the same TSMC process for their NVHBM base dies. It also requested sixth-generation DRAM technology for the memory core dies, the report said.

The approach aims to make products from different suppliers perform consistently and reduce the work required to validate each supplier’s memory. Samsung accepted the requirements following an internal review, the newspaper reported.

NVHBM, unveiled in August, incorporates Nvidia’s custom memory controller into the base die. That component sits beneath the stacked memory chips and contains logic circuitry governing data transfers.

The reported cooperation brings together two competitors in contract chip manufacturing as Nvidia seeks a more consistent supply of specialised memory for its computing platforms.

Samsung has traditionally manufactured both the memory core and base die itself. It intends to retain that integrated production model for standard HBM products and customised memory supplied to other customers, including AMD, according to the newspaper.

Samsung is also assessing whether its own foundry could manufacture NVHBM base dies if demand exceeds TSMC’s available capacity, the report added.

The development suggests that customer requirements are reshaping relationships across the semiconductor supply chain, encouraging rivals to cooperate on selected components while continuing to compete elsewhere.

The manufacturing plans remain attributed to the newspaper’s sources; the report should therefore be distinguished from a formal joint announcement.
